title: Animal body plans: rings, two halves, spirals and segments

summary.text: A starfish has five arms in a ring, while a cat has two matching sides. Why do animals have such different body shapes? In this unit you will test whether matching sides help a roller go straight, collect animals with the same plan, and find four tissues in your hand.
summary.art: A crow, a fish, an ant and a child seen from above, each with a faint line down the middle, and beside them a jellyfish seen from above as a ring with the mouth in the centre.

intro.hook: A starfish has five arms and no head. So which way is forwards for a starfish?
intro.text: Any way is forwards for a starfish. She can walk with any arm in front. You are built differently. Your eyes, nose and mouth are all at one end, and you walk that end first. Your left side matches your right, but your front does not match your back. Animal bodies are laid out in a few ways: in rings, in two halves, in spirals and in rows of repeated parts. In this unit you find out what each layout is good for. You roll a lopsided roller made of dough and a pencil. You tilt a tall dough shell and a coiled one. You also find four kinds of tissue in your own hand.
intro.art: A five-armed starfish on a rock pool floor seen from above, with five small arrows pointing outwards along the five arms.

outcomes: I can say what a body plan is, and name four plans: rings, two halves, spirals and segments.
I can explain radial symmetry, and why it suits an animal who stays in one place or drifts.
I can explain bilateral symmetry, and why an animal who travels has a head end and matching sides.
I can test fairly whether matching sides help a roller go straight, and say what my results show.
I can find segments in a worm, a prawn, an insect and my own backbone. I can say what repeating is good for.
I can explain how a snail's shell grows into a spiral. I can test why a coil is easier to carry than a tall cone.
I can say what a tissue is, name the four kinds in animals, and find them in my own hand.
I can explain why a similar shape does not prove that two animals are close relatives.

terms.meaning: The basic layout of an animal's body: which parts there are, and how they are arranged.
terms.example: A fish and a crow share one body plan. Each has a head end, a tail end and two matching sides.
terms.art: A fish and a crow drawn side by side from above, each with a line down the middle.

terms.meaning: A shape has symmetry when one part of it matches another part.
terms.example: Your left hand matches your right hand. That is symmetry.
terms.art: Two open hands side by side, palms down, with a dotted line between them.

terms.meaning: Matching parts arranged round a middle point, like the spokes of a cycle wheel.
terms.example: A sea anemone has a ring of tentacles round her mouth.
terms.art: A sea anemone seen from above, with tentacles spreading out from a mouth in the centre.

terms.meaning: One line down the middle of the body, with a matching left side and right side.
terms.example: An ant, a gecko and a human all have bilateral symmetry.
terms.art: A house gecko on a wall seen from above, with one dotted line from nose to tail.

terms.meaning: The front end of a two-sided animal, where the eyes, feelers, mouth and brain are gathered.
terms.example: A fish swims head end first, so her eyes and mouth meet the water first.
terms.art: A fish swimming to the left with the eyes and mouth circled at the front.

terms.meaning: One of a row of repeated parts along a body, each built on the same pattern.
terms.example: Each ring of an earthworm is one segment.
terms.art: An earthworm on damp soil with the rings along the body clearly drawn.

terms.meaning: A line that winds round a middle point and moves further out with every turn.
terms.example: A snail's shell is a spiral. So is a murukku.
terms.art: A garden snail's shell seen from the side, with a line drawn along the coil from the tip to the opening.

terms.meaning: The young form of an animal, when the young looks very different from the adult.
terms.example: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly. A starfish larva is a tiny swimmer with two sides.
terms.art: A tiny clear starfish larva with two matching sides, drawn large, next to a small adult starfish.

terms.meaning: An animal who lives fixed in one place, with a body full of small holes and no head or mouth.
terms.example: Natural bath sponges are the soft skeletons of sea sponges.
terms.art: A vase-shaped sea sponge on a reef, with small arrows showing water going in at the sides and out at the top.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that every living body is made of.
terms.example: Your body has about thirty trillion cells. That is 30 lakh crore.
terms.art: A sheet of skin cells seen through a microscope, packed side by side like floor tiles.

terms.meaning: A group of cells of the same kind that are joined together and do one job.
terms.example: Muscle is a tissue. All the cells in a muscle shorten together to pull.
terms.art: A bundle of long thin muscle cells lying side by side, all pointing the same way.

terms.meaning: A body part built from several tissues that work together.
terms.example: Your heart is an organ. It has muscle tissue, nerve tissue and a smooth lining.
terms.art: A human heart with small labels pointing to the muscle wall and the lining.

terms.meaning: An instruction for building part of a body, passed from parents to their young.
terms.example: Genes called Hox genes mark out a body from head to tail.
terms.art: A fly and a mouse, each with a row of coloured bands from head to tail in the same order.

explanations.concept: A body plan is the basic layout of a body
explanations.definition: A body plan is the basic layout of an animal's body: which parts there are, and how they are arranged.
explanations.description: Scientists have named more than a million kinds of animals. Yet almost all of them are built on a few layouts. Three questions sort most animals. Does the body have a front end? Do the left and right sides match? Are there parts that repeat in a row? A jellyfish has no front end, and her parts are arranged in a ring. A fish has a front end and two matching sides. An earthworm has a front end, matching sides and about a hundred repeated rings. A snail has a front end and matching sides, and she carries a shell that coils in a spiral. Humans are animals too. We have a front end, matching sides and a row of repeated bones down the back. This unit takes the plans one at a time. It also looks inside, at the tissues that every plan is built from.
examples: Rings: a sea anemone on a rock at Rameswaram.
Two halves: a crow, a rohu fish, a house gecko and you.
Segments: an earthworm, a centipede and a prawn.
A spiral: the shell of a garden snail.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a sea anemone, a crow, a centipede and a snail, each with the pattern of the body drawn over the animal in red.

explanations.concept: Bodies built in rings: radial symmetry
explanations.definition: Radial symmetry means that matching parts are arranged round a middle point, like the spokes of a cycle wheel.
explanations.description: A sea anemone is fixed to a rock. Her mouth is on top, in the middle, with a ring of tentacles round it. Food may drift towards her from any side, and so may danger. So her body is the same all the way round, and every side is ready. A jellyfish has the same plan turned upside down. Her mouth hangs under the middle of the bell, and tentacles hang from the rim. She drifts and pulses, and she meets the water equally on every side. A ring body has a top and a bottom. It has no front, no back, no left and no right. Cut it through the middle along many different lines, and the two halves match. Ring animals have no head. Their nerve cells are spread through the body as a net, so the whole body senses and responds. Corals are ring animals too. Each coral animal, called a polyp, is like a tiny sea anemone sitting in a stone cup.
examples: A sea anemone in a rock pool catches a shrimp who touches any tentacle.
A moon jellyfish has four matching parts round the middle of her bell.
The corals of the Gulf of Mannar and Lakshadweep are built by millions of tiny ring-shaped polyps.
explanations.art: A sea anemone fixed to a rock, seen from the side, with small arrows of drifting food coming towards her from every direction.

explanations.concept: Bodies built in two halves: bilateral symmetry
explanations.definition: Bilateral symmetry means that a body has one line down the middle, with a matching left side and right side.
explanations.description: A two-sided body has three pairs of opposite sides: front and tail, back and belly, and left and right. The front end differs from the tail end. The back differs from the belly. Only the left and the right match. So there is exactly one line that cuts the body into matching halves. An animal with this plan moves front end first. The front end meets food, danger and new places before the rest of the body does. So the eyes, the feelers, the nose and the mouth are gathered there, with a brain close behind them. That gathered front end is a head. Worms, insects, spiders, crabs, snails, fish, frogs, birds and mammals all have this plan. Out of every hundred kinds of animals, about ninety-nine are two-sided. The matching is on the outside. Inside a human, the heart leans to the left and the liver lies on the right.
examples: A house gecko runs up the wall head first, with two matching legs on each side.
A dragonfly has two matching pairs of wings and two huge eyes at the front.
You have two eyes, two ears, two arms and two legs, and one nose on the middle line.
explanations.art: A dragonfly seen from above with a dotted line from head to tail, and the labels front, tail, left and right.

explanations.concept: Why animals who travel have matching sides
explanations.definition: The usual explanation is that matching sides give equal pushes, so the animal travels straight.
explanations.description: An animal moves by pushing on the ground, the water or the air. Legs, fins and wings come in pairs, one on each side. If the left side pushed harder than the right, the animal would curve to the right. She would have to correct her path at every step. With matching sides the pushes are equal, and the path is straight. In the Lopsided Roller test you see this with a pencil and two balls of dough. The roller with equal balls goes nearly straight, and the roller with unequal balls curves. Top and bottom do not match in animals, because gravity pulls down and the ground is on one side only. Front and back do not match, because the animal goes one way. Left and right are the only pair that meet the same conditions. This is the usual explanation. It is hard to test on living animals, so scientists still argue about how two-sided bodies first arose.
examples: A rowing boat with one oar goes round in a circle.
A fish has a matching fin on each side of her body.
Most birds drop the same feather from each wing at the same time, so the two wings stay equal.

perspectives.who: Gábor Holló and Mihály Novák, in a paper of 2012
perspectives.explanation: Matching sides let an animal travel straight and also turn quickly to either side. Two-sided bodies have lasted because they steer well.

perspectives.who: John Finnerty, in a paper of 2005
perspectives.explanation: Two sides may first have helped the inside of the body, by giving food and water a clear path through. Easy travel may have come later.

explanations.art: A fish seen from above swimming straight, with two equal arrows pushing back from the two sides of the tail.

explanations.concept: A starfish starts with two sides and becomes a star
explanations.definition: A larva is the young form of an animal, when the young looks very different from the adult.
explanations.description: An adult starfish has five arms round a middle, with the mouth underneath. She has no head that anyone can see, and any arm can lead when she walks. So a starfish looks like a ring animal. But a starfish egg hatches into a tiny, clear larva who swims in the open sea. The larva has a front end and two matching sides. After some weeks a small five-part star grows inside the larva. The star settles on the sea floor, and the rest of the larva's body shrinks away. Sea urchins grow up the same way. This tells us that the ancestors of starfish were two-sided animals, and the star shape came later. The ring of a starfish and the ring of a jellyfish arose separately. Starfish are closer relatives of fish and humans than of jellyfish. So the same shape does not prove that two animals are close relatives. Scientists also compare the young, and they compare the genes.
examples: A starfish larva is smaller than a grain of rice and swims with tiny beating hairs.
A sea urchin's round shell has five matching parts, and her larva has two matching sides.
A dolphin and a shark have a similar shape. A dolphin is a mammal and a shark is a fish, so the shape does not make them close relatives.
explanations.art: Three drawings in a row with arrows between them: a tiny two-sided starfish larva, the same larva with a small star growing inside, and a young five-armed starfish.

explanations.definition: A segment is one of a row of repeated parts along a body, each built on the same pattern.
explanations.description: An earthworm's body is a row of about a hundred rings. Each ring is a segment with muscles and tiny bristles of its own. The worm squeezes a few segments at a time, and so she moves through the soil. A centipede has one pair of legs on each segment. A millipede has two pairs on most of hers. Repeating has two uses. A body can grow long by making the same part again and again. And a segment can be changed to do a new job. A prawn shows this well. Some of her segments carry feelers, some carry jaws, some carry walking legs and some carry swimming legs. An insect's body is made of segments joined into three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. The thorax is the middle part. It has three segments with one pair of legs each, which is why an insect has six legs. You are built in segments too. Run a finger down your backbone and feel the row of bumps. Each bump is one bone of the row, and your ribs repeat in pairs.
examples: A cooked fish breaks into flakes. Each flake is one block of muscle, and the blocks repeat from head to tail.
The tail part of a prawn has six segments that you can count at the fish market.
A human backbone starts as 33 small bones in a row.
explanations.art: A prawn seen from the side with each segment drawn in a different shade, and the feelers, walking legs and swimming legs labelled.

explanations.concept: Bodies with a spiral: the snail's shell
explanations.definition: A spiral is a line that winds round a middle point and moves further out with every turn.
explanations.description: A snail's soft body has a head, two matching sides and a flat foot. Her shell is different. A snail never leaves her shell, and she never sheds one. As she grows, she adds new shell only at the opening, where her body meets the edge. Each new part is a little wider than the part before it. The shell also curves as it grows, so it winds round and round. The tiny tip in the middle is the shell she hatched with. If the shell grew straight, a big snail would carry a long, tall cone. A coil packs the same room into a low, compact shape, which is easier to carry. In Tall Cone or Coil you test this with dough. Most snail shells coil to the right. Hold a shell with the tip up and the opening facing you. If the opening is on your right, the shell is right-handed. The chank shell, or sangu, blown at temples is the shell of a sea snail. A chank that coils the opposite way is very rare. In Tamil it is called a valampuri sangu, and people prize it.
examples: A garden snail on a wet wall in the monsoon carries a shell with four or five turns.
The apple snail of paddy fields has a round, right-handed shell.
A shaligram stone from the Gandaki river in Nepal holds a coiled ammonite shell. Ammonites were sea animals who died out long ago.
explanations.art: A garden snail on a leaf, with the tip of the shell labelled oldest part and the rim of the opening labelled newest part.

explanations.concept: Sponges: animals with no fixed shape
explanations.definition: A sponge is an animal who lives fixed in one place. Her body is full of small holes, and she has no head or mouth.
explanations.description: A sponge lives fixed to a rock or a reef. Most sponges grow as a lump, a crust or a vase, and no two are quite alike. Water flows in through thousands of tiny holes and out through a few large ones. Cells lining the inside beat tiny hairs to keep the water moving, and they catch bits of food from it. A sponge has several kinds of cells, but she has no muscles, no nerves and no gut. Even so, a sponge senses what touches her and can slowly squeeze her whole body. In 1907 the American scientist H. V. Wilson pressed a living sponge through fine silk cloth. The sponge came apart into separate cells in a dish of sea water. Over the next days the cells crawled back together and built small new sponges. So each cell can find the others and take up a job again. For a long time people classed sponges with plants. In the 1820s Robert Grant in Edinburgh watched sponges pump water through their bodies, and showed that they are animals.
examples: A natural bath sponge is the soft skeleton of a sea sponge.
Sponges of many colours grow on the reefs of the Andaman Islands.
A sponge the size of a tumbler can pump many buckets of sea water in a day.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a vase-shaped sponge, with arrows showing water entering through small holes in the wall and leaving through the large opening at the top.

explanations.concept: Tissues: groups of cells that do one job together
explanations.definition: A tissue is a group of cells of the same kind that are joined together and do one job.
explanations.description: Every animal is made of cells, which are the tiny living units of a body. One cell is far too small to see. A human body has about thirty trillion of them, which is 30 lakh crore. Cells of one kind join up to make a tissue. Animals have four main kinds of tissue. Covering tissue makes sheets, such as the outside of your skin and the lining of your mouth. Scientists call it epithelial tissue. Connecting tissue holds parts together and supports them. Bone, fat, blood and the cords called tendons are all connecting tissues. Scientists call them connective tissue. Muscle tissue is made of long cells that can shorten, and it pulls parts so that they move. Nerve tissue carries signals quickly from one part of the body to another. Several tissues together make an organ, such as a heart, a stomach or an eye. So the order is cell, tissue, organ, whole animal. A snail, a prawn and a human are laid out very differently. Yet all three are built from the same four kinds of tissue.
examples: The mound at the base of your thumb is muscle tissue. It goes hard when you pinch.
The cords that move on the back of your hand are tendons, a connecting tissue.
The meat of a fish is muscle tissue, and the skin is covering tissue.
explanations.art: A drawing of a hand with four small circles zooming in on skin cells, muscle cells, a tendon and a nerve.

explanations.concept: Why are there so few body plans?
explanations.definition: Most body plans alive today were already present about 540 million years ago, and scientists argue about why.
explanations.description: Rocks about 540 million years old hold the first clear fossils of most animal groups alive today. This time is called the Cambrian. Animals with rings, with two sides, with segments and with shells were all there. Since then, many kinds of animals have appeared and died out. But almost no new body plan has appeared. In the 1980s scientists also found something surprising. Flies, mice and humans use the same family of genes to mark the body from head to tail. These are called Hox genes. A gene is an instruction for building part of a body, passed from parents to their young. Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard and Eric Wieschaus found many of the genes that lay out a fly's segments. They shared a Nobel Prize in 1995 with Edward Lewis. So very different bodies are laid out by very similar instructions. Why the plans are so few, and so old, is still argued.
examples: A fly's Hox genes sit in the same order as the body parts they mark, from head to tail.
A mouse has matching genes that mark out her neck, chest and tail in the same order.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how bodies grow
perspectives.explanation: The layout is set very early, when the young animal is only a few cells. A change that early upsets everything built afterwards, so the plan stays.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study ways of life
perspectives.explanation: The main ways of making a living were taken long ago. A new plan would have to compete with animals who are already good at each one.

perspectives.who: Stephen Jay Gould, in his book Wonderful Life (1989)
perspectives.explanation: Chance played a large part. Many early plans died out, and if history ran again a different set might survive.

perspectives.who: Simon Conway Morris, in his book Life's Solution (2003)
perspectives.explanation: Similar ways of life lead to similar bodies again and again. If history ran again, the plans would turn out much the same.

explanations.art: A fly and a mouse, each with a row of coloured bands along the body in the same order, and a matching row of coloured blocks below each animal.

agreed.text: Nearly all kinds of animals have a front end and two matching sides.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have named more than a million kinds of insects, spiders, crabs, worms, snails and animals with backbones. All of these are two-sided.

agreed.text: A starfish begins life as a larva with two matching sides.
agreed.evidence: Johannes Müller watched starfish and sea urchin larvae change into stars in the 1840s. Anyone with a microscope can watch the same change today.

agreed.text: Animal bodies are made of cells, and the cells are grouped into tissues.
agreed.evidence: Around 1800 the French doctor Xavier Bichat sorted the materials of the body into tissues. In 1839 Theodor Schwann showed with a microscope that animal tissues are made of cells.

agreed.text: Separated sponge cells can come together again and rebuild a sponge.
agreed.evidence: H. V. Wilson showed this in 1907, and many scientists have repeated the test since.

agreed.text: Flies, mice and humans use the same family of genes to mark out the body from head to tail.
agreed.evidence: In the 1980s scientists read these Hox genes in flies. They then found matching genes in mice, frogs and humans.

agreed.text: In pond snails, one gene of the mother decides which way a young snail's shell coils.
agreed.evidence: Breeding tests published in 1923 showed this pattern. In 2019 Reiko Kuroda's team in Japan switched the gene off, and the young snails coiled the opposite way.

challenging.claim: Starfish and jellyfish belong in one group, because both are built in rings.
challenging.who: Georges Cuvier, in his book on the animal kingdom of 1817.
challenging.for: Both have matching parts round a middle, and neither has a head that anyone can see.
challenging.against: A starfish larva has two matching sides, and a small star grows inside the larva. Genes also show that starfish are closer relatives of fish than of jellyfish.

challenging.claim: Every two-sided animal has matching left and right sides.
challenging.for: Most animals look matched from the outside.
challenging.against: A flatfish begins life matched. Then one eye moves across the head, and the adult lies on one side. A male fiddler crab has one huge claw. Inside a human, the heart, stomach and liver are not matched.

challenging.claim: All animals share one body plan. An insect is laid out like an animal with a backbone, turned upside down.
challenging.who: Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, who argued this against Cuvier in Paris in 1830.
challenging.for: In the 1990s scientists found that the same genes mark the belly and the back in flies and in frogs. The genes sit on opposite sides in the two animals, as if one of them were turned upside down.
challenging.against: Cuvier pointed to real differences. An insect's skeleton is on the outside, and the main nerve cord runs along the belly. Most scientists say the plans are related but are not one plan.

challenging.claim: All the animal body plans appeared suddenly, about 540 million years ago.
challenging.who: A common reading of the Cambrian fossils.
challenging.for: Most animal groups first show up as clear fossils in rocks of about that age.
challenging.against: Older rocks hold earlier animals. Ikaria, a two-sided animal the size of a rice grain, lived about 555 million years ago. Scott Evans, Mary Droser and their team described the fossils in 2020. Soft bodies rarely become fossils, so the start may be older still.

challenging.for: No end of a starfish has eyes, a brain and a mouth together, and any arm can lead.
challenging.against: In 2023 Laurent Formery and his team mapped the genes at work in a young starfish. Genes that mark the head in other animals were switched on along every arm. Genes that mark the trunk were mostly missing.

big_questions.q: A starfish larva has two sides, and the adult is a star. Are they the same animal?
big_questions.hint: Think about what stays the same when a body changes its whole layout.

big_questions.q: Your left and right sides match on the outside but not on the inside. Which is your real plan?
big_questions.hint: Your two arms match, and yet your heart leans to the left.

big_questions.q: If animals lived where there was no up or down, what body plans might they have?
big_questions.hint: On Earth, gravity makes the top differ from the bottom in almost every animal.

big_questions.q: Is a body plan a real thing in nature, or a way that people sort animals?
big_questions.hint: Cuvier's group of ring animals looked right for thirty years. Then starfish larvae showed that it was two groups.

big_questions.q: Cars, boats and planes have matching sides. Did people copy animals, or did they meet the same problem?
big_questions.hint: In the Lopsided Roller test, the roller with unequal balls curved on every roll. Think about what would happen to a car with a stronger wheel on one side.

big_questions.q: Each of your cells is alive. So are you one living being, or trillions living together?
big_questions.hint: H. V. Wilson's sponge cells lived apart in a dish, and then rebuilt a sponge.

story.title: The Boat with No Front
story.note: Ponni, her grandmother and her cousin are made up. These facts are real: round bamboo boats called parisal, or coracles, are used on the Kaveri river at Hogenakkal in Tamil Nadu. A parisal is woven from split bamboo and covered underneath with a tarred sheet. The paddler kneels at the rim and pulls the water towards her, and any part of the rim can lead.
text: Ponni was ten, and she was ashamed of her grandmother's boat.

It was a parisal, as round as a dosa pan and wide enough for six people. Paati had woven it herself from split bamboo and covered the bottom with a tarred sheet. It had no pointed end and no back end. It had no left and no right. It sat on the Kaveri at Hogenakkal like a basket that someone had dropped.

In the summer holidays Ponni had stayed with her cousin Devika near Alappuzha. The boats there were long and narrow, with a raised nose at one end. They went down the canals as straight as a line of thread.
"A boat should know which way it is going," Ponni said when she came home.
Paati did not argue. She held out the paddle. "Take us across, then."

So every evening, in the slow green water above the falls, Ponni practised. She knelt at the rim and pulled the paddle through the water on her right. The parisal turned to the right, and went on turning. She paddled on her left. The parisal turned to the left. In a quarter of an hour she had made nine circles and travelled about the length of a goat.
"It only spins," she said.
"It spins because you paddle beside it," said Paati. "Reach out in front of your knees and pull the water straight towards you. Then the place where you kneel is the front."

Ponni tried. The parisal wobbled forwards, slowly, like a plate being pushed across a table. It was better than spinning. But she thought of Devika's long boat cutting down the canal, and she was not comforted.
Then the rain came to the hills upstream. For two days the Kaveri ran brown and quick. On the third morning Paati said the fish traps had to be lifted before the river took them.

The traps were tied among the black rocks below the bathing place. There the river split into narrow channels, and the water did not agree with itself. It pushed from the left in one place and from the right in the next. Paati knelt at the rim and worked the parisal into a channel hardly wider than the boat. Rock stood on both sides, close enough to touch.
At the end of the channel the first trap hung on its rope. Paati put down the paddle and took the rope in both hands. The trap was heavy with water and weed. She leaned back and hauled.
Ponni looked back the way they had come. A tree branch as long as a bus was coming down the channel towards them. It turned slowly as it came, and its wet twigs scraped along the rock.
"Paati," she said.
"I see it. My hands are full. Take us out by the side gap, there, behind you."
Ponni snatched up the paddle. The side gap was behind her left shoulder. She did what anyone on Devika's canal would do. She began to turn the boat round, to point its front at the gap.
The rim struck rock. She pushed off and tried the other way. The rim struck rock again. There was no room to turn anything. The branch was four boat-lengths away, then three.
Ponni stared at the round rim of the parisal. Every part of it looked the same. There was nothing to point.
Then she understood that there was nothing to turn, either.

She let the boat be. She crawled across the bamboo floor to the part of the rim nearest the gap, knelt there, reached the paddle out in front of her knees and pulled. The parisal did not swing round. It simply went that way, as if that part of the rim had always been the front. They slid sideways out of the channel and into the gap. Behind them the branch went past with a long scraping sound, and the water closed over the place where they had been.
Paati dropped the trap into the boat. Three small fish jumped inside the trap. She looked at Ponni for a moment and then went back to coiling the rope.

That evening the river was quieter. Ponni sat on the steps with her feet in the water. Near her toes a row of small fish held their place in the current. Every one of them pointed the same way, nose to the flow, and the two sides of each fish matched like the two sides of Devika's boat. When a shadow crossed them they shot off upstream, straight and fast, all in one direction.

A leaf came down the river, turning. Then the parisal came past, with Paati kneeling at the rim, bringing a neighbour's children home. A boy in the boat dropped his cap in the water on the far side. Paati did not turn the boat. She moved along the rim and pulled, and the parisal went to the cap.
On Sunday Devika telephoned. "Does your round boat still not know where it is going?" she asked.
"It does not need to know," said Ponni. "I know. And wherever I kneel, that is the front."
story.epiphany: A long boat has one front. It goes fast and straight, but it needs room to turn. A round boat is the same on every side, so any part of the rim can lead. Animal bodies are built in the same two ways. A fish is built to go one way, head first. A sea anemone or a jellyfish is the same all the way round. She is ready on every side at once.
ask: Why could the round boat leave the narrow channel without turning round?
Which animals are built like the long boat, and which like the round boat?
When would a body with no front be more useful than a body with a head?
