games.title: Plan Families: collect five animals with one body plan
games.context: This is a card game about body plans. You collect sets of five animals whose bodies are laid out in the same way.

setup.art: Twenty small cards spread on a table, each with the name of an animal and a short description.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 20 animal cards. Shuffle them.

setup.art: Two players each holding five cards, with a pile of cards face down between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal five cards to each player. Put the rest in a pile.

setup.art: A child laying five cards in a row on the table: jellyfish, sea anemone, coral polyp, starfish and sea urchin.
setup.caption: 3. Ask for a plan. Collect all five animals of one family and lay them down.

printables.title: 20 animal cards: the animal and what the body is like
items: Moon jellyfish. A soft bell. The mouth hangs under the middle, and tentacles hang all round the rim.
Sea anemone. Fixed to a rock. One mouth on top, with tentacles all round it.
Coral polyp. Tiny, sitting in a stone cup. Tentacles all round one mouth.
Starfish. Five arms round a mouth in the middle. Any arm can lead.
Sea urchin. A spiny ball with five matching parts round the mouth underneath.
Rohu fish. A head end and a tail end. One eye and one side fin on each side.
Frog. A head with two eyes in front. Two matching short legs and two matching long legs.
Crow. A beak at the front. Two matching wings and two matching feet.
House gecko. Runs head first up a wall on four matching feet. A tail at the back.
Human. A face at the front. Two matching arms and two matching legs.
Garden snail. Carries a coiled shell and adds to it at the opening.
Apple snail. Lives in paddy fields. A round shell that winds to a small tip.
Chank, or sangu. A heavy white sea shell that winds round and is blown like a horn.
Nautilus. A sea animal with many arms and a coiled shell divided into rooms.
Ammonite. A coiled shell turned to stone, from a sea animal who died out long ago.
Earthworm. A long soft body made of about a hundred rings in a row.
Centipede. A long row of parts, with one pair of legs on each part.
Millipede. A long row of hard rings, with two pairs of legs on most rings.
Prawn. A row of parts with feelers, walking legs, swimming legs and a tail fan.
Caterpillar. A soft body of rings in a row, with stubby legs on some rings.

printables.title: 4 plan families: the answer sheet
items: Rings (parts round a middle): moon jellyfish, sea anemone, coral polyp, starfish, sea urchin.
Two halves with a head and a backbone: rohu fish, frog, crow, house gecko, human.
A spiral shell: garden snail, apple snail, chank, nautilus, ammonite.
A row of segments: earthworm, centipede, millipede, prawn, caterpillar.

rules: There are four families: rings, two halves with a backbone, a spiral shell, and a row of segments. Each family has five cards.
Deal five cards to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile. Keep the answer sheet face down.
On your turn, ask one player for a plan you already hold. For example: 'Do you have any animals built in rings?'
If they have any, they give you all of them, and you take another turn. If they have none, take the top card of the pile.
When you hold all five cards of one family, lay them down. Say what the five bodies share.
The game ends when all four families are on the table. The player with the most families wins. Check them against the answer sheet.
Playing alone? Shuffle the cards and sort them into four families as fast as you can. Then check the answer sheet. Try to beat your time.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the answer sheet. Shuffle the cards. Read the names of the four families aloud.
flow.say: Each card describes the body of one animal. There are four families of five. A family shares one body plan: rings, two halves, a spiral shell or a row of segments.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Learn the names of the four families.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plan Families. You set up the cards and learn the four families.

flow.do: Deal five cards each and play. With one child, the parent is the second player. Let your child read each new card aloud.
flow.say: Ask me for a plan you already hold. If I have any animals with that plan, I must give them all to you.
flow.kid: Ask for a plan you hold. Collect all five of a family.

ask.q: How did you decide which family a card belongs to?
good: I looked for a head end.
I asked whether the parts go round a middle.
I looked for parts that repeat in a row.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: does this animal have a front end? If not, the card belongs to the rings.
flow.context: In this step of Plan Families you play the first half of the game and start to collect families.

flow.do: Play on until all four families are on the table. Each time a family is laid down, the player says what the five share.
flow.say: You have all five. Before you lay them down, tell me what these five bodies have in common.
flow.kid: Lay down each full family. Say what the five bodies share.
flow.context: In this step of Plan Families you finish the game and say what each family shares.

flow.do: Turn over the answer sheet and check the four families. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the snails and the row of segments. Do those animals also have a head end and matching sides?
flow.kid: Check the answer sheet. Which families also have a head end?

check.q: A centipede is built in segments. Does a centipede also have two matching sides?
options: Yes, a left side and a right side
No, only segments
No, a centipede is a ring
check.why: Yes. A centipede has a head end and matching left and right legs on every segment. Segments are an extra pattern inside a two-sided body. A body can follow more than one pattern at once.

flow.context: This is the last step of Plan Families. You check the families and compare them.

games.title: Sit or Seek: a dice game of two bodies in two seas
games.context: This is a dice game with two model animals. One is built in a ring and one has a front. You find out which body eats more in two kinds of sea.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a grid of five rows of five squares, the middle square marked with a star, and N, E, S and W written on the four edges.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 5 rows of 5 squares. Mark the middle square. Write N, E, S and W on the four edges.

setup.art: A small round ball of dough and a small dough animal with a pointed head, beside a die and a heap of rajma beans.
setup.caption: 2. Make a round ring animal and a front animal with a pointed head.

setup.art: The dough animal with a head on the middle square, facing the edge marked N, with one rajma bean on the square in front of her.
setup.caption: 3. In the drifting sea, the die says which side the food comes from.

setup.art: The grid with eight rajma beans on the corner squares and the middle squares of the edges, and the dough animal moving towards one.
setup.caption: 4. In the still sea, the food stays put. The animal must go to the food.

printables.title: The sea: a grid you draw
items: Draw 5 rows of 5 squares on a sheet of paper. Make each square about 4 centimetres wide.
Mark the middle square with a star. Every round starts there.
Write N on the top edge and E on the right edge. Write S on the bottom edge and W on the left edge.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Drifting sea, ring animal: food eaten in 12 turns ____
Drifting sea, front animal: food eaten in 12 turns ____
Still sea, ring animal: food eaten in 12 turns ____
Still sea, front animal: food eaten in 12 turns ____

rules: You need one die, 12 rajma beans or groundnuts as food, and two dough animals. The ring animal is a round ball. The front animal has a pointed head.
There are four rounds of 12 turns. Every round starts with the animal on the middle square.
Drifting sea. Each turn, roll the die. A 1 brings food from N, a 2 from E, a 3 from S and a 4 from W. A 5 or a 6 brings no food.
The ring animal has arms on every side. She eats every piece of food that arrives.
The front animal has one mouth, at her head. She eats only food that arrives on the side she faces. After each roll she may turn to face a new side.
Still sea. Put 8 beans on the board: one on each corner square, and one on the middle square of each edge. No die is needed for the front animal.
In the still sea, the front animal takes one action each turn. She either steps one square forwards or turns to face a new side. She eats a bean when she lands on that square.
In the still sea, the ring animal creeps slowly. Roll the die each turn. Only on a 6 may she move one square, in any direction.
Write each score on the score sheet. With two players, each plays all four rounds, and the higher total wins.

flow.do: Draw the grid and make the two dough animals. Read the rules together. Ask for a guess before the first roll.
flow.say: One animal is round, with arms on every side. The other has a head and one mouth. Which will eat more when food drifts in from all sides? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw the grid. Make two dough animals. Which will eat more? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Sit or Seek. You set up the board and guess which body will eat more.

flow.do: Play the drifting sea. Play 12 turns with the ring animal, then 12 turns with the front animal. Write both scores.
flow.say: Roll the die. Which side did the food come from? Did your animal catch the food? For the front animal, choose which way to face next.
flow.kid: Roll 12 times for each animal. Write how much each one ate.
flow.parent: The ring animal usually eats about 8 pieces in 12 turns. The front animal usually eats about 2. Luck will move these numbers up or down.
flow.context: In this step of Sit or Seek you play the drifting sea, where food arrives from any side.

flow.do: Play the still sea. Put out the 8 beans. Play 12 turns with the front animal, then 12 turns with the ring animal. Write both scores.
flow.say: Now the food does not come to you. Plan a path for the front animal. Remember that a turn uses up one action.
flow.kid: Put out 8 beans. Play 12 turns for each animal. Write both scores.
flow.parent: A front animal with a good path eats 3 or 4 beans. The ring animal usually eats 0 or 1.
flow.context: In this step of Sit or Seek you play the still sea, where food stays in one place.

flow.do: Look at the four scores together. Ask which body won in each sea.
flow.say: Which body ate more in the drifting sea? Which ate more in the still sea? Where do real sea anemones live, and where do real fish hunt?
flow.kid: Look at your four scores. Which body won in each sea?

check.q: In Sit or Seek, which sea suits an animal who is the same on every side?
options: The sea where food drifts in from all sides
The sea where food stays far away
Both seas equally
check.why: A ring body is ready on every side, so drifting food is caught wherever it arrives. In the still sea the ring animal is too slow to reach the food. A front body does better there, because she can travel to it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sit or Seek. You compare the ring animal and the front animal in the two seas.

experiments.title: The Lopsided Roller: do matching sides help a body go straight?
experiments.question: A roller is made of a pencil with a ball of dough on each end. Does it roll straight when the two balls match? What happens when one ball is smaller than the other?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which roller will go straightest? Will a lopsided roller turn towards the big ball or towards the small ball? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same dough and pencils of the same length for all three rollers. Push each pencil about 1 centimetre into each ball. Start every roll from the same line on the same ramp, and let go without pushing. Keep the small ball on the right for the main rolls. Roll each roller 5 times, because one roll can be a fluke. Only one thing changes: how well the two balls match.
results_table: Roll 1 to roll 5: how many centimetres from the line, and on which side

materials.item: stiff atta dough made from about one and a half cups of atta, or modelling clay
pencils of about the same length (or straight sticks cut to the same length)
a tray, a chopping board or a large hardbound book, to make a ramp
a thin book about 3 centimetres thick, to raise one end of the ramp
a smooth floor with about one and a half metres of clear space
a ruler, a piece of chalk or string for the line, and a little dry flour
a notebook page and a pencil for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows: matched roller, a little lopsided, very lopsided. For each roll, write how far from the line the roller stopped, and on which side. If the roller went right round, write 'circle'.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three rollers from pencils and balls of dough. You test whether a roller needs matching sides to roll straight.

setup.art: Three pencils on a table, each with a ball of dough pushed on to each end: one with two equal balls, one with a large and a medium ball, one with a large and a very small ball.
setup.caption: 1. Make three rollers. Balls of 4 and 4 centimetres, 4 and 3 centimetres, and 4 and 2 centimetres.

setup.art: A tray resting with one end on a thin book, on a tiled floor, with a chalk line running straight out from the middle of the low end.
setup.caption: 2. Raise one end of a tray on a book. Draw a straight line on the floor from the ramp.

setup.art: A child holding the matched roller across the top of the ramp with one finger on each ball.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the roller across the top of the ramp. Let go without pushing.

setup.art: The lopsided roller on the floor at the end of a curved path, with a ruler measuring the gap between the roller and the chalk line.
setup.caption: 4. Where the roller stops, measure how far it is from the line, and on which side.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows and five numbers in each row, some marked left and some marked right.
setup.caption: 5. Roll each roller 5 times. Write every result.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: centimetres from the line where the roller stopped
rows: A little lopsided: 4 cm and 3 cm

flow.do: Show your child a pencil and two lumps of dough, one large and one small. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will put a ball of dough on each end of a pencil and let it roll. Which roller will go straightest? Will a lopsided one turn towards the big ball or the small ball? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which roller goes straightest. Which way will a lopsided roller turn? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will turn that way?
good: The big ball is heavier.
The big ball goes further each time it turns.
The small ball is slower.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children expect the roller to turn towards the big ball.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lopsided Roller test. You guess how matched and lopsided rollers will roll, before you test.

flow.do: Make four balls 4 centimetres wide, one ball 3 centimetres wide and one ball 2 centimetres wide. Check each against the ruler. Push a pencil about 1 centimetre into each ball to make the three rollers. Dust the balls with dry flour.
flow.say: Roll each ball between your palms until it is round. Hold it beside the ruler to check the size. The two balls of the matched roller must be as equal as you can make them.
flow.kid: Roll six balls of dough. Check each size with the ruler. Push them on to the pencils.
flow.parent: Stiff dough works best. If the dough is sticky, knead in more dry atta. For the matched roller, make one lump and cut it exactly in half. That gives two equal balls.
flow.context: In this step of the Lopsided Roller test you make three rollers from dough and pencils.

flow.do: Rest one end of the tray on the thin book. Draw a chalk line on the floor, straight out from the middle of the low end, about 1 metre long. Mark a start line across the top of the ramp.
flow.say: This line shows where a roller would go if it rolled perfectly straight. We will start every roll from the same place.
flow.kid: Make the ramp. Draw a straight line on the floor from the ramp.
flow.parent: A line between two rows of floor tiles can be the straight line. If the rollers stop too soon, raise the ramp on a second book.
flow.context: In this step of the Lopsided Roller test you set up the ramp and the straight line on the floor.

flow.do: Hold the matched roller across the start line, with its middle over the chalk line. Let go. Where it stops, measure from its middle to the chalk line. Write the distance and the side. Do this 5 times.
flow.say: Let go gently, with no push. Where did the middle of the roller stop? How far is that from the line, and on which side?
flow.kid: Roll the matched roller 5 times. Measure how far from the line it stops.
flow.parent: The matched roller usually stops within about 10 centimetres of the line, sometimes left and sometimes right. No hand-made roller is perfectly matched.
flow.context: In this step of the Lopsided Roller test you roll the roller with two equal balls 5 times.

flow.do: Roll the roller with the 4 centimetre and 3 centimetre balls 5 times, with the small ball on the right. Measure and write each result. Then do the same with the 4 centimetre and 2 centimetre roller.
flow.say: Watch the path. Is it a straight line or a curve? Which ball is on the inside of the curve?
flow.kid: Roll the two lopsided rollers 5 times each. Watch which way they curve.

check.q: In the Lopsided Roller test, which way did the roller with unequal balls curve?
options: Towards the side with the small ball
Towards the side with the big ball
A different way on every roll
check.why: The roller curves towards the small ball. In one full turn the big ball rolls further along the floor than the small ball. So the big ball's side gets ahead, and the roller swings round the small ball. If you chose 'the big ball', look again at which ball is on the inside of the curve.

flow.parent: The 4 and 3 roller makes a wide curve to the right. The 4 and 2 roller turns in a tight circle and may come back towards the ramp. Write 'circle' for that.
flow.context: In this step of the Lopsided Roller test you roll the two rollers with unequal balls.

flow.do: Turn the 4 and 3 roller round, so that the small ball is on the left. Roll it 3 times. Then add dough to the small ball until it is 4 centimetres wide, and roll it 3 more times.
flow.say: Now the small ball is on the left. Which way will it curve this time? Now we make the small ball match the big one. What will happen?
flow.kid: Put the small ball on the left. Roll it. Then make both balls match and roll again.
flow.parent: With the small ball on the left, the roller curves left. That shows the curve comes from the roller and not from the floor. Once the balls match, the roller goes nearly straight again.
flow.context: In this step of the Lopsided Roller test you swap the sides, and then you make the two balls match.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your results. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me: why might a fish need two matching sides?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the lopsided roller curve?
good: The big ball goes further in one turn.
One side moved faster than the other.
The two sides were not equal.

ask.q: What would happen to a fish whose left fins pushed harder than her right fins?
good: She would swim in a curve.
She would keep turning to the right.
She would have to keep correcting her path.

flow.parent: The reason: both balls are fixed to one pencil, so they turn together. In one turn a 4 centimetre ball rolls about 12 and a half centimetres along the floor. A 3 centimetre ball rolls only about 9 and a half. So the big ball's side gets ahead, and the roller curves towards the small ball. An animal's legs, fins or wings work in the same way. If one side pushes more than the other, the animal curves. With matching sides, the pushes are equal and the path is straight. The roller is a model, and a living animal can also correct her own path.
flow.think: A rowing boat has two oars. What happens if only one person rows, on one side?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lopsided Roller test. You say what your results show about matching sides.

experiments.title: Tall Cone or Coil: which shell is easier to carry as it grows?
experiments.question: A snail's shell must get bigger as the snail grows. If the shell grew as a straight cone, would a taller cone fall over more easily? Does the same amount of shell stay on better when it is coiled?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Three dough cones are 6, 9 and 12 centimetres tall. Which will fall over first when the board is tilted? Will a coil made from the same dough as the tallest cone fall sooner or later? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Make every cone 3 centimetres wide at the base, and press each base flat. Stand each cone at the same spot on the same board. Lift the same end of the board slowly each time, about one finger-width each second. Measure the height of the lifted end at the moment the cone falls. Test each shape 3 times. For the coil, use exactly the dough of the 12 centimetre cone. Only the shape changes.
results_table: Height of the lifted end when the shape fell: try 1, try 2 and try 3
The middle value of the three tries

materials.item: stiff atta dough, about one cup (the dough from the Lopsided Roller test can be used again), or modelling clay
a chopping board, a tray or a large hardbound book, about 30 centimetres long
a ruler
a sheet of paper to cover the board if the dough slides
a notebook page and a pencil for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows: the 6 centimetre cone, the 9 centimetre cone, the 12 centimetre cone and the coil. Write the height of the lifted end for each of the three tries. If a shape did not fall, write 'did not fall' and the height you reached.
experiments.context: In this experiment you make dough models of snail shells: three straight cones and one coil. You tilt a board to find out which shape falls over first.

setup.art: Three dough cones standing in a row on a table, 6, 9 and 12 centimetres tall, each with a base 3 centimetres wide, with a ruler standing beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make three cones, 6, 9 and 12 centimetres tall. Each base is 3 centimetres wide.

setup.art: The shortest dough cone standing on a chopping board while a child lifts one end of the board and an adult holds a ruler upright at that end.
setup.caption: 2. Stand a cone on the board. Lift one end slowly. Read the ruler when the cone falls.

setup.art: A long thin tapering rope of dough being wound into a flat coil like a murukku.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the tallest cone into a long thin cone. Wind it into a flat coil.

setup.art: The dough coil lying on the tilted board, still in place, with the lifted end of the board high above the table.
setup.caption: 4. Tilt the board with the coil on it. Does it fall?

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: height of the lifted end when the shape fell
rows: Coil made from the 12 cm cone

flow.do: Show your child a snail shell or a picture of one, and a lump of dough. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: A snail's shell is a long cone that is wound into a coil. We will test straight cones and a coil on a tilted board. Which will fall first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which dough shell will fall first on a tilted board. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Tall Cone or Coil. You guess which shell shape will fall over first, before you test.

flow.do: Make three dough cones, 6, 9 and 12 centimetres tall. Make each base 3 centimetres wide. Press each base on the table so that it is flat and the cone stands upright.
flow.say: Shape each cone like a carrot standing on its thick end. Check the height and the base with the ruler.
flow.kid: Make three dough cones: 6, 9 and 12 centimetres tall. Flatten each base.
flow.parent: If the tallest cone bends over, the dough is too soft. Knead in more dry atta and shape it again.
flow.context: In this step of Tall Cone or Coil you make three straight cones of different heights.

flow.do: Stand the 6 centimetre cone in the middle of the board. Your child lifts one end slowly. You hold the ruler upright at that end. Read the height when the cone falls. Do this 3 times. Then test the 9 centimetre cone and the 12 centimetre cone in the same way.
flow.say: Lift slowly, about one finger-width each second. Stop the moment the cone tips. I will read the height.
flow.kid: Lift one end of the board slowly. Stop when the cone falls. Write the height.
flow.parent: If a cone slides before it falls, lay a sheet of paper on the board and try again. The shortest cone needs the steepest tilt.
flow.context: In this step of Tall Cone or Coil you tilt the board under each of the three straight cones.

flow.do: Take the 12 centimetre cone. Roll it into a long thin cone about 25 centimetres long. Wind it into a flat coil, with the thin tip in the middle. Lay the coil flat on the board and tilt the board 3 times.
flow.say: This coil is made of exactly the same dough as the tallest cone. Lift the board again. Does the coil fall at the same height?
flow.kid: Roll the tallest cone long and thin. Wind it into a coil. Tilt the board again.

check.q: In Tall Cone or Coil, the coil was made from the dough of the tallest cone. Why?
options: So that only the shape was different
So that the coil was heavier
So that less dough was wasted
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. The coil and the tall cone have the same amount of dough, so any difference comes from the shape. If you chose 'heavier', remember that the same dough weighs the same in any shape.

flow.parent: The coil usually stays in place until the board is very steep, and then it slides. Write 'did not fall' and the height you reached.
flow.context: In this step of Tall Cone or Coil you turn the tallest cone into a coil and test it.

flow.do: For each shape, circle the middle value of the three tries. Put the four shapes in order, from the one that fell first to the one that fell last.
flow.say: Which shape fell at the lowest tilt? Which stayed on longest? What happened as the cones got taller?
flow.kid: Circle the middle value for each shape. Which shape fell first?
flow.context: In this step of Tall Cone or Coil you put the four shapes in order of steadiness.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me: what would a straight shell be like for a big, old snail?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why does a taller cone fall over at a smaller tilt?
good: More of it is high up.
It leans past its base sooner.
The base is the same but the cone is taller.

ask.q: Why does the coil stay on?
good: It is low and wide.
All the dough is close to the board.

flow.parent: In most homes the 12 centimetre cone falls first and the 6 centimetre cone last. The coil does not fall at all. The reason: a tall cone has much of its weight high above a small base. A small tilt carries that weight past the edge of the base, and the cone falls. A coil keeps the same amount of shell low and close to the board. A snail's shell grows only at the opening, so a straight shell would become a longer and longer cone. Scientists think that coiling keeps a growing shell compact and easy to carry.
flow.think: A snail adds shell only at the opening. Where on the shell is the part she made as a baby?
flow.context: This is the last step of Tall Cone or Coil. You say what your results show about straight shells and coiled shells.

activities.title: Three Pairs of Sides: which sides of a body match?

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a steel tumbler
a window or balcony where a crow, a pigeon, an ant or a gecko can be seen

schedule.what: Check three pairs of sides on yourself, on one other animal and on a tumbler.

activities.record: A table with three rows: me, another animal, and the tumbler. It has three columns: top and bottom, front and back, left and right. Write 'match' or 'differ' in each box.
activities.context: In this activity you check three pairs of sides on yourself, on another animal and on a steel tumbler. You find out which pairs match.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows labelled Me, Another animal and Tumbler, and three columns labelled Top and bottom, Front and back, Left and right.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with three rows and three columns.

setup.art: A child standing in front of a mirror touching her left ear with her left hand and her right ear with her right hand.
setup.caption: 2. Check your own body. Which pairs of sides match?

setup.art: A child at a window looking at a crow on a railing, with a notebook in her hand.
setup.caption: 3. Check one other animal you can see.

setup.art: A steel tumbler standing upside down on a table, with a child turning it slowly round.
setup.caption: 4. Turn a tumbler upside down. This is the shape of a jellyfish. Check the tumbler's sides.

flow.do: Draw the table. Your child stands up and compares three pairs of sides of their own body: top and bottom, front and back, left and right.
flow.say: Compare your head end with your feet. Do they match? Now compare your front with your back. Now compare your left side with your right side.
flow.kid: Compare your top and bottom. Then front and back. Then left and right.

good: Only left and right.
My two arms and two legs match.
My front and back are different.

flow.context: This is the first step of Three Pairs of Sides. You check which sides of your own body match.

flow.do: Find one other animal: a crow or pigeon outside, an ant, a gecko, a fly or a pet. Check the same three pairs. If no animal is near, use a toy animal or a picture on a packet.
flow.say: Look at this animal's three pairs of sides. Which pair matches? Where are the eyes and the mouth?
flow.kid: Find another animal. Check the three pairs of sides. Where are the eyes?
flow.parent: Humans count as animals, so a family member will do. Every animal your child can find at home will have only left and right matching.
flow.context: In this step of Three Pairs of Sides you check the sides of one other animal you can see.

flow.do: Stand the tumbler upside down. Explain that a jellyfish is shaped like this, with the mouth under the middle and tentacles round the rim. Check the three pairs on the tumbler.
flow.say: This tumbler stands for a jellyfish. Does the top match the bottom? Turn it slowly. Can you find a front, a back, a left or a right?
flow.kid: Turn a tumbler upside down. Does it have a front? Does it have a left side?

check.q: A crow has a front and a back. Which pair of a crow's sides match each other?
options: Left and right
Front and back
Top and bottom
check.why: Only the left and the right match. A crow's front has a beak and eyes, and her back end has a tail. Her top faces the sky and her belly faces the ground. If you chose 'front and back', compare the beak with the tail.

flow.parent: The tumbler has a top and a bottom, but it is the same all the way round. That is radial symmetry. Every animal your child checked had only one matching pair, left and right. That is bilateral symmetry.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Pairs of Sides. You check the sides of a tumbler that stands for a jellyfish.

activities.title: Four Tissues in Your Hand

materials.item: your own hand
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a sheet of paper and a pencil
a feather or a short piece of thread

schedule.what: Find covering tissue, muscle tissue, connecting tissue and nerve tissue in your own hand, and label a drawing.

activities.record: Trace round your hand on paper. Label where you found each of the four kinds of tissue: covering, muscle, connecting and nerve.
activities.context: In this activity you find the four main kinds of animal tissue in your own hand: covering tissue, muscle tissue, connecting tissue and nerve tissue.

setup.art: A child looking at the back of her hand through a magnifying glass, with the fine lines of the skin drawn large in a circle.
setup.caption: 1. Look closely at your skin. It is a sheet of covering tissue.

setup.art: A child pressing the fleshy mound at the base of her thumb with a finger of the other hand while pinching thumb and first finger together.
setup.caption: 2. Pinch hard. Feel the muscle at the base of your thumb go firm.

setup.art: The back of a hand with the fingers wiggling and thin cords showing under the skin from the knuckles to the wrist.
setup.caption: 3. Wiggle your fingers. Watch the cords move on the back of your hand.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed while a parent touches one fingertip lightly with a feather.
setup.caption: 4. Close your eyes. Feel a feather touch one finger.

setup.art: A pencil outline of a hand on paper with four labels and arrows.
setup.caption: 5. Trace your hand. Label the four tissues.

flow.do: Look at the back of the hand closely, with a magnifying glass if you have one. Put one drop of water on the skin and watch it.
flow.say: Your skin is a sheet that covers you. Look at the fine lines. Does the drop of water soak in or sit on top? A tissue that covers a surface is called covering tissue.
flow.kid: Look closely at your skin. Put a drop of water on it. What does the drop do?
flow.parent: The drop sits on top. The outer skin is many layers of flat cells packed closely together, and it keeps water out.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Tissues in Your Hand. You look at your skin, which is covering tissue.

flow.do: Your child rests one hand on the table, palm up. With the other hand, they press the mound at the base of the thumb. Then they pinch thumb and first finger together hard.
flow.say: Press the soft mound at the base of your thumb. Now pinch hard. What happens to the mound? That is muscle tissue. Its cells have all shortened at once.
flow.kid: Press the mound below your thumb. Now pinch hard. What do you feel?

good: It went hard.
It got fatter and firmer.
It bulged.

flow.context: In this step of Four Tissues in Your Hand you feel muscle tissue at the base of your thumb.

flow.do: Your child holds the hand flat, palm down, and wiggles the fingers as if playing a keyboard. Look for cords moving under the skin. Then press a knuckle and feel the bone.
flow.say: See the cords that move? They are tendons. Each one ties a muscle in your arm to a finger bone. Tendons and bones are connecting tissues.
flow.kid: Wiggle your fingers. Watch the cords on the back of your hand. Press a knuckle.
flow.parent: The muscles that move the fingers are mostly in the forearm. Ask your child to hold their forearm and wiggle the fingers, and they will feel those muscles working.
flow.context: In this step of Four Tissues in Your Hand you find tendons and bone, which are connecting tissues.

flow.do: Your child closes their eyes. Touch one fingertip very lightly with the feather or thread. Ask which finger was touched. Then press on a fingernail for 3 seconds and let go.
flow.say: Eyes closed. Which finger did I touch? You knew at once, because nerve tissue carried a signal to your brain. Now watch your nail. It goes white, then pink again, as the blood comes back.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Which finger was touched? Then press your nail and watch the colour.
flow.parent: Blood is a connecting tissue too, although it is liquid. Its cells float in a watery fluid and travel to every part of the body.
flow.context: In this step of Four Tissues in Your Hand you test nerve tissue with a light touch. You also watch blood return under a nail.

flow.do: Trace round the hand on paper. Label the four tissues and where each was found.
flow.say: Label your drawing: covering tissue, muscle tissue, connecting tissue and nerve tissue. Which did you see, and which did you only feel?
flow.kid: Trace your hand. Label where you found each of the four tissues.

check.q: In Four Tissues in Your Hand, the mound at the base of your thumb went firm when you pinched. Which tissue is it?
options: Muscle tissue
Covering tissue
Nerve tissue
check.why: It is muscle tissue. Muscle cells are long, and they shorten together when you pinch, so the mound bunches up and feels firm. Covering tissue is the skin over the mound. Nerve tissue carried the order to pinch.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Tissues in Your Hand. You label a drawing of your hand with the four kinds of tissue.

activities.title: One Segment, Many Times: a paper chain animal

materials.item: a strip of paper about 30 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide
scissors
a pencil and colour pencils

schedule.what: Fold a paper strip, draw one segment, cut once and get a row of eight. Then change some segments to do new jobs.

activities.record: Keep the paper animal. On the back, write what job you gave to each changed segment.
activities.context: In this activity you draw one body segment and cut it once from folded paper. You get a row of eight matching segments, and then you change some of them.

setup.art: A long strip of paper folded backwards and forwards like a fan into eight equal parts.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the strip backwards and forwards into 8 equal parts.

setup.art: The folded stack of paper with one drawing on top: an oval that touches both folded edges, with one small leg above and one below.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one segment. The oval must touch both folded edges.

setup.art: A child cutting round the drawing through all the layers, leaving the folded edges uncut where the oval touches them.
setup.caption: 3. Cut round the drawing. Do not cut the folds where the oval touches them.

setup.art: The paper opened out into a row of eight joined ovals, each with a pair of legs, with eyes and feelers drawn on the first and a tail fan on the last.
setup.caption: 4. Open it out. Change the first and last segments.

flow.do: Fold the paper strip backwards and forwards, like a fan, into 8 equal parts. Press the folds flat.
flow.say: We are going to build a long animal by drawing only one part. How many times do you think we will need to cut?
flow.kid: Fold the strip like a fan into 8 equal parts.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Segment, Many Times. You fold a paper strip into eight parts.

flow.do: On the top layer, draw an oval that touches both folded edges. Add one leg above and one leg below. Cut round the drawing through all the layers. Leave the folds joined where the oval touches them.
flow.say: Draw one segment with one pair of legs. Now cut through all the layers at once. Keep the two sides of the oval joined at the folds.
flow.kid: Draw one oval with two legs. Cut it out. Do not cut the folds.
flow.parent: Eight layers of notebook paper are stiff to cut. Help with the scissors if your child's hand gets tired.
flow.context: In this step of One Segment, Many Times you draw one segment and cut it out of the folded paper.

flow.do: Open the paper out. Count the segments and the legs.
flow.say: You drew one segment. How many did you get? How many legs? An earthworm grows a long body in this way, by making one kind of part again and again.
flow.kid: Open the paper. Count the segments. Count the legs.

ask.q: You drew one pair of legs. How many legs does the animal have?
good: 16 legs.
8 pairs, because there are 8 segments.

flow.context: In this step of One Segment, Many Times you open the paper chain and count the segments.

flow.do: Change some segments. Draw eyes and long feelers on the first one and trim its legs short. Snip the last one into a tail fan. Colour a few middle segments as walking legs and a few as swimming legs.
flow.say: A prawn's segments began alike, and each kind now does a different job. Change your segments. Which will sense, which will walk and which will swim?
flow.kid: Give the first segment eyes and feelers. Make the last a tail. Colour the rest.

check.q: A prawn has feelers, walking legs and swimming legs on different segments. What does this show?
options: Repeated parts can be changed for new jobs
Each part was invented separately
Prawns have no segments
check.why: Each of these parts grows from one segment, and all the segments are built on one pattern. A body can copy a part many times and then change some copies for other jobs. If you chose 'invented separately', look at your paper animal. Every part began as the same oval.

flow.context: This is the last step of One Segment, Many Times. You change the matching segments so that they do different jobs.

activities.title: Prawn, Fish and Shell: body plans in the kitchen (if your family buys prawns or fish, or has a sea shell)

materials.item: a whole raw prawn, a piece of cooked fish, or a snail shell or chank shell
a plate
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Count the segments of a prawn or the muscle blocks of a fish, and find which way a shell coils.

activities.record: Draw what you looked at. Write the number of segments or muscle blocks you counted. For a shell, write whether the opening is on the right or the left.
activities.safety: Wash hands with soap after touching raw prawn or fish.
activities.context: In this activity you look for segments in a prawn or a piece of fish. You also look for the spiral in a real shell. Do it only if your family has one of these at home.

setup.art: A whole raw prawn on a steel plate with a child's finger pointing at the rings of the tail part.
setup.caption: 1. Count the rings on the tail part of a prawn.

setup.art: A piece of cooked fish on a plate breaking into curved flakes under a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Or press a piece of cooked fish. Count the flakes.

setup.art: A hand holding a snail shell with the tip pointing up and the opening facing the viewer, the opening on the right side.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a shell with the tip up and the opening facing you. Which side is the opening on?

flow.do: Put the prawn on a plate. Count the rings of the tail part, and look under each ring for a pair of small legs. If you have cooked fish, press the piece gently and count the flakes in a row.
flow.say: How many rings can you count on the tail part? What is under each ring? In the fish, what shape is each flake?
flow.kid: Count the rings on the prawn's tail part. Look under each ring.
flow.parent: The tail part of a prawn has six segments. The first five carry a pair of small swimming legs each, and the sixth carries the tail fan. Each flake of a cooked fish is one block of muscle. The blocks repeat from head to tail.
flow.context: This is the first step of Prawn, Fish and Shell. You count the segments of a prawn or the muscle blocks of a fish.

flow.do: Hold the shell with the tip pointing up and the opening facing your child. Ask which side the opening is on. Then trace the coil with a finger from the tip to the opening.
flow.say: The tip is the oldest part of the shell. Trace the coil from the tip to the opening. Is the opening on your right or your left?
flow.kid: Hold the shell tip up. Is the opening on your right or left? Trace the coil.

check.q: Where is the oldest part of a snail's shell?
options: At the tip, in the middle of the coil
At the rim of the opening
The whole shell is the same age
check.why: The tip is the oldest part. A snail adds new shell only at the opening, so the rim is the newest part. The tip is the shell she hatched with. If you chose 'the rim', remember that the rim is where the growing happens.

flow.parent: Nearly every shell you find will have the opening on the right. That is a right-handed shell. A left-handed one is rare.
flow.context: This is the last step of Prawn, Fish and Shell. You find the oldest part of a shell and which way the shell coils.

projects.title: My Body Plan Album: twelve animals in four days

materials.item: six sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small book, or a notebook
a pencil, a red pencil and a ruler

schedule.what: Draw three animals you can see at home or from the window. Mark the front and the middle line.
Draw three animals from the kitchen, the market or a food packet.
Draw three sea animals from a book or a screen: one ring animal, one snail and one of your choice.
Draw three more animals. Then sort all twelve by body plan and make a contents page.

projects.record: One page for each animal. Draw the animal from above. Mark the front end with an F. Draw every line that cuts the body into matching halves in red. Write the body plan, and the number of segments if you can count them.
projects.context: In this four-day project you make an album of twelve animals. For each one you find the front end, the lines of matching halves and the body plan.

setup.art: A small hand-made book open at a page with a pencil drawing of an ant from above, a red line from head to tail and a letter F at the head.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one animal on each page, seen from above. Mark the front with an F.

setup.art: A page with a drawing of a starfish from above and five red lines through the centre.
setup.caption: 2. Draw in red every line that cuts the body into matching halves.

setup.art: A contents page with four headings, Rings, Two halves, Spiral shell and Segments, and animal names listed under each.
setup.caption: 3. On the last day, sort all twelve animals by body plan.

flow.do: Day 1. Find three animals at home or from the window. An ant, a crow, a gecko, a fly or a family member will do. Draw each from above on a page of its own. Mark the front and the red line.
flow.say: Draw the animal as if you were looking down from the ceiling. Where is the front? How many lines cut this body into matching halves?
flow.kid: Draw three animals from above. Mark the front. Draw the middle line in red.
flow.parent: A quick, rough drawing is enough. The point is the front end and the red line, not a perfect picture.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Body Plan Album. You draw three animals you can see and find the middle line of each.

flow.do: Day 2. Find three animals in the kitchen, at the market or on a food packet: a fish, a prawn, a crab or a hen. Draw each and mark the front and the red line. Count any segments.
flow.say: Does this animal have parts that repeat in a row? Count them if you can.
flow.kid: Draw three animals from the kitchen or market. Count any repeated parts.
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Body Plan Album. You draw three animals from the kitchen or the market and look for segments.

flow.do: Day 3. From a book or a screen, choose a jellyfish or a starfish, a snail, and one more sea animal. Draw each from above. A ring animal will need several red lines.
flow.say: How many red lines can you draw through a starfish? How many through a snail's shell?
flow.kid: Draw a jellyfish or starfish, a snail and one more. How many red lines?
flow.parent: A starfish has five lines of matching halves. A snail's coiled shell has none, although her soft body has one.
flow.context: This is day 3 of My Body Plan Album. You draw three sea animals, with at least one ring animal and one snail.

flow.do: Day 4. Draw three more animals of your child's choice. Then write a contents page that sorts all twelve under four headings: rings, two halves, spiral shell and segments. An animal can go under two headings.
flow.say: Which heading has the most animals? Did any animal fit two headings? Did any animal fit none?
flow.kid: Draw three more. Sort all twelve by body plan. Which plan has the most?

check.q: Twelve animals are found at home and at the market. Which body plan is likely to be the most common?
options: Two matching halves
Rings
A spiral shell
check.why: Two matching halves. About ninety-nine of every hundred kinds of animals are two-sided. Every animal who walks, flies or swims past a home is two-sided. Ring animals live in water, mostly in the sea.

flow.context: This is day 4 of My Body Plan Album. You sort all twelve animals by body plan.

challenges.title: Many Threads, One Lift: build a model tendon from sewing thread
challenges.problem: A tendon ties a muscle to a bone. It is a tissue made of thousands of thin fibres lying side by side. One fibre alone is weak. Your problem is similar, because one sewing thread alone is weak too. It snaps when it lifts a bag that weighs 2 kilograms. Lift the bag with thread alone, using as few threads as you can.
constraints: Use ordinary sewing thread only. No string, wool or tape.
Each thread is 30 centimetres long before you tie it.
The bag must hang 2 centimetres above the floor for 10 seconds.
Lift slowly. Do not jerk the bag.
materials: a reel of ordinary sewing thread
a cloth bag with handles, holding a 2 kilogram packet of rice or two full 1 litre bottles
a rolling pin or a strong ladle to tie the threads to
a notebook page and a pencil
general: Tie several threads side by side between the rolling pin and the bag's handles.
Make every thread the same length, so that each one takes a share of the weight.
Spread the threads along the rolling pin so that they do not rub on each other.
creative: Twist the threads together into one cord, as fibres are twisted in a rope.
Plait three groups of threads, as hair is plaited.
Tie short threads in two rows, so that if one thread snaps the others still hold.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Find the smallest number of threads that holds the bag for 10 seconds. Draw how you arranged them. Then test one change, such as twisting, and write whether you needed fewer threads.
challenges.context: In this challenge you lift a 2 kilogram bag using only thin sewing thread. It is a model of a tendon, a tissue made of many thin fibres that share one job.

setup.art: A cloth bag with a packet of rice in it on the floor, a reel of sewing thread, scissors and a rolling pin.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 kilograms in a cloth bag. Cut threads 30 centimetres long.

setup.art: One thread tied from a rolling pin to the handles of the bag, snapping as a child lifts the rolling pin.
setup.caption: 2. Try one thread first. Lift slowly, just above the floor.

setup.art: Six threads tied side by side from the rolling pin to the bag's handles, all the same length, holding the bag just above the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Add threads side by side. Make them the same length.

setup.art: A notebook drawing of the rolling pin, the threads and the bag, with the number of threads written beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Find the smallest number of threads that holds for 10 seconds.

flow.do: Put the packet in the bag. Tie one 30 centimetre thread from the rolling pin to both handles. Your child lifts the rolling pin slowly until the bag is just off the floor.
flow.say: A tendon is made of thousands of thin fibres. Here one thread stands for one fibre. Will one thread hold the bag? Lift slowly, and keep your feet back.
flow.kid: Tie one thread to the bag. Lift slowly. Does one thread hold?
flow.parent: Most sewing thread snaps at about 1 kilogram or less, and a knot makes it weaker. If one thread does hold, add another kilogram to the bag. Keep the bag close to the floor so that it cannot fall far.
flow.context: This is the first step of Many Threads, One Lift. You test whether a single thread can lift the 2 kilogram bag.

flow.do: Tie 3 threads side by side and test. If they snap, try 4, then 5. Each time, look at which thread snapped first.
flow.say: Try three threads. Did they all snap together, or did one go first? Look at the lengths. Which thread was tightest?
flow.kid: Tie three threads side by side. Lift. Which thread snaps first?

ask.q: Why did one thread snap before the others?
good: It was shorter, so it took all the weight.
The others were loose.
They were not sharing the weight.

flow.parent: The shortest thread goes tight first and carries the whole bag for a moment. It snaps, and then the next shortest does the same. Equal lengths are what make the threads share.
flow.context: In this step of Many Threads, One Lift you add threads side by side and watch which one snaps first.

flow.do: Let your child choose their own design. They may match the lengths carefully, twist the threads or plait them. Test each design for 10 seconds.
flow.say: Now use your own idea. How will you make every thread take a share? Count ten seconds aloud while the bag hangs.
flow.kid: Build your own design. Lift the bag. Count to ten.
flow.context: In this step of Many Threads, One Lift you build and test your own way of sharing the weight.

flow.do: Write the smallest number of threads that held. Draw the design. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: How many threads did you need? Your tendons work in the same way. Thousands of thin fibres lie side by side, all the same way, and share the pull.
flow.kid: Write how many threads held the bag. Draw your design.

check.q: In Many Threads, One Lift, one thread snapped but several equal threads held the bag. How is that like a tissue?
options: Many alike cells share one job
One big cell does all the work
Each cell does a different job
check.why: A tissue is many cells of one kind doing one job together. In a tendon or a muscle the fibres lie the same way. Each takes a small share of the pull. One fibre alone would snap, as one thread did.

flow.context: This is the last step of Many Threads, One Lift. You record your best design and compare it with a tendon.

items.p: What is a body plan?
opts: The basic layout of an animal's body
A list of what an animal eats
The place where an animal lives
The colour of an animal's skin
items.why: A body plan says which parts a body has and how they are arranged. Two animals with very different colours and homes can share one body plan.

items.p: Which animal has matching parts arranged all the way round a middle point?
items.why: A sea anemone has a ring of tentacles round one mouth. A crow, an earthworm and a gecko each have a head end and two matching sides.

items.p: An animal with one head end and matching left and right sides has ____ symmetry.
items.why: Bilateral symmetry means two matching sides. There is exactly one line that cuts such a body into matching halves.

items.p: A jellyfish has a left side and a right side.
items.why: False. A jellyfish is the same all the way round, so no part of her is a left or a right. She has a top and a bottom only.

items.p: Match each animal to their body plan.
pairs: Two matching halves with a backbone
items.why: Ask three questions. Does the body have a front end? Do the sides match? Do parts repeat in a row? The snail also carries a coiled shell.

items.p: Sort these animals. Does each one have a head end?
items: fish
Has a head end
ant
Has a head end
frog
Has a head end
jellyfish
Has no head end
sea anemone
Has no head end
sponge
Has no head end
items.why: An animal who travels front end first has eyes and a mouth gathered at that end. Animals who drift or stay fixed have no front, so they have no head.

items.p: In the Lopsided Roller test, the roller with one big ball and one small ball curved. Why?
opts: The big ball rolls further each turn
The floor slopes to one side
items.why: Both balls turn together on one pencil. In one turn the big ball covers more floor than the small ball. So the big ball's side gets ahead, and the roller curves.

items.p: Insects, prawns and centipedes all have bodies built in segments.
items.why: True. All three have a row of repeated parts. In an insect the segments are joined into a head, a thorax and an abdomen.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest to the largest.
items: a cell
a tissue
an organ
a whole animal
items.why: Cells of one kind make a tissue. Several tissues make an organ. Many organs make a whole animal.

items.p: A group of cells of the same kind that do one job together is called a ____.
items.why: Muscle, nerve, covering tissue and connecting tissue are the four main kinds of tissue in animals.

items.p: Where does a snail add new shell as she grows?
opts: At the rim of the opening
Nowhere. She finds a new shell
items.why: A snail's body touches the shell at the opening, so new shell is added there. The tip is the oldest part. A snail never changes shells.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why a sea anemone has tentacles all round her body.
items.a: A sea anemone is fixed to a rock, and food can drift towards her from any side. Tentacles all round mean that every side is ready to catch it.
items.why: A strong answer links the ring shape to a life in one place. There, food and danger come from every side.

items.p: In Tall Cone or Coil, the tall dough cone fell over first. What does this suggest about snail shells?
items.a: A straight shell would become a tall cone as the snail grew, and the cone would tip over easily. A coiled shell keeps the same amount of shell low and steady.
items.why: A strong answer uses the result of the test: the taller the cone, the sooner it fell, and the coil stayed on.

items.p: Draw an ant from above. Draw the one line that cuts the ant into matching halves.
items.a: An ant seen from above. One straight line runs from the head to the tail end, through the middle of the body. Three legs and one feeler are on each side of the line.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the line from head to tail. A line across the middle is wrong, because the front half and the back half do not match.
items.art: A blank box with a faint outline of an ant seen from above.

items.p: When you bend your thumb, which tissue is pulling?
items.why: Muscle tissue is the only tissue whose cells can shorten and pull. Bone is pulled, and skin covers the muscle.

worksheets.title: Why bodies are laid out this way

items.p: An animal lives fixed to a rock, and food drifts in from every side. Which plan suits her best?
opts: A ring of arms round the mouth
A long body with one head
A spiral shell with a lid
items.why: Food can arrive from any side, so a body that is the same all the way round catches the most. In Sit or Seek, the ring animal ate most in the drifting sea.

items.p: Why are an animal's eyes, nose and mouth usually at the front end?
opts: The front meets new things first
The front is the heaviest part
items.why: An animal who travels meets food and danger with her front end first. Senses placed there give the earliest warning.

items.p: A young starfish has two matching sides.
items.why: True. A starfish larva has a front end and two matching sides. The five-part star grows inside the larva later.

items.p: Starfish and jellyfish are close relatives, because both are built in rings.
items.why: False. Starfish larvae are two-sided, and starfish are closer relatives of fish than of jellyfish. The two ring shapes arose separately.

items.p: Sort these animals. Can you see a row of segments on the outside of the body?
items: earthworm
Segments can be seen
centipede
Segments can be seen
prawn
Segments can be seen
caterpillar
Segments can be seen
jellyfish
No segments can be seen
sea anemone
No segments can be seen
items.why: A segmented body has parts that repeat in a row from head to tail. A ring animal's parts repeat round a middle instead.

items.p: Three of these animals have a spiral shell. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A prawn has a hard covering made of segments in a row. The garden snail, the chank and the nautilus each carry one coiled shell.

items.p: An insect's middle part has 3 segments. Each segment carries one pair of legs. How many legs is that?
items.why: One pair is 2 legs, and 3 times 2 is 6. That is why every insect has six legs.

items.p: Match each tissue to its job.
pairs: Makes a sheet over a surface
Holds parts together and supports them
items.why: Each tissue is a group of alike cells with one job. Bone, blood, fat and tendons are all connecting tissues.

items.p: Put the life of a starfish in order.
items: An egg floats in the sea
A tiny larva with two matching sides swims
A small five-part star grows inside the larva
The small star settles on the sea floor
The adult walks on five arms
a: An egg floats in the sea
A tiny larva with two matching sides swims
A small five-part star grows inside the larva
The small star settles on the sea floor
The adult walks on five arms
items.why: The two-sided larva comes first and the star grows inside. This order shows that the ancestors of starfish were two-sided.

items.p: The matched roller in the Lopsided Roller test drifted either way. The lopsided roller always curved one way. Why?
items.a: The matched roller had no built-in turn. Its small drifts came from chance, such as a bump or an uneven let-go. The lopsided roller had a big ball on one side, so it was pulled round the same way every time.
items.why: A strong answer separates chance from cause. Chance goes either way. A cause built into the shape goes the same way on every roll.

items.p: The tip of a snail's shell is the oldest part. Explain why.
items.a: A snail adds new shell only at the opening. So the first shell she made is pushed further and further from the opening. It ends up as the tip in the middle of the coil.
items.why: A strong answer says where the shell grows. Any answer that puts the growth at the opening is on the right track.

items.p: A sponge has many cells but no muscles or nerves. Name one thing a sponge can still do.
items.a: A sponge can pump water through her body and catch food from it. She can also sense a touch and slowly squeeze her body. Her separated cells can come back together.
items.why: A strong answer gives something sponges are known to do. Pumping water, sensing touch and rebuilding from separate cells all count.

items.p: A starfish has five arms and no head that anyone can see. Scientists describe her body in different ways.

views.says: The adult has five matching arms round a middle. We should call the starfish a ring animal.

views.who: A scientist who studies young animals
views.says: The larva has a front end and two matching sides. The starfish belongs with the two-sided animals.
Head genes are switched on along every arm, and trunk genes are mostly missing. So most of a starfish's body is built like a head, with almost no trunk.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that the adult shape is what we can see and count. Another is that the larva shows where starfish came from. Another is that genes show what each part is built as.
items.why: Each view uses real evidence. A strong answer says what kind of evidence it trusts most, and takes one other view seriously.

items.p: Label four sides of this fish: front end, tail end, back and belly.
a: Front end: where the mouth and eyes are
Tail end: where the tail fin is
Back: the upper side, towards the surface
Belly: the lower side, towards the river bed
items.why: A two-sided body has a front and a tail that differ, and a back and a belly that differ. The left and right sides are the only pair that match.
items.art: A side view of a rohu fish facing left, with four blank label lines pointing to the head, the tail fin, the upper side and the lower side.

items.p: An adult flatfish lies on one side, with both eyes on the upper side. What does this show?
opts: Not every two-sided animal stays matched
items.why: A young flatfish has matching sides. As she grows, one eye moves across her head. Body plans have exceptions, and they can change during one life.

items.p: Two animals share a ring shape. What is the best way to check whether they are close relatives?
opts: Compare their young and their genes
items.why: Shape alone can mislead, as it did with starfish and jellyfish. Young forms and genes carry more of an animal's family history.

items.p: A lopsided roller curves left. You add dough to the small ball until both balls match. What should happen?
opts: The roller curves left more sharply
The roller curves right in a circle
items.why: The curve came from the unequal balls. With equal balls, both sides cover the same distance in each turn, so the path is straight.

items.p: Sponge cells were pushed apart through cloth. Over some days they crawled together again. What does this show?
opts: Sponge cells can find their own kind
items.why: Each cell moved, met other sponge cells and joined them. H. V. Wilson first showed this in 1907.

items.p: A prawn's segments carry feelers, jaws, walking legs and swimming legs. What does this show about segments?
opts: Repeated parts can change for different jobs
Every segment must stay the same
items.why: All these parts grow from segments built on one pattern. Repeating a part and then changing some copies gives a body many tools.

items.p: The same family of genes marks out head to tail in a fly and in a human.
items.why: True. These are the Hox genes. Finding them in such different animals was strong evidence that all two-sided animals share an ancestor.

items.p: Inside a human body, the heart and the liver are placed the same on the left and the right.
items.why: False. The heart leans to the left and the liver lies on the right. Humans match on the outside but not fully on the inside.

items.p: Match each way of life to the body plan that suits it.
pairs: Fixed to a rock, with food drifting from all sides
Two matching halves with a head
Burrowing by squeezing one part at a time
Carrying a house that must grow with the body
items.why: Each layout fits a way of meeting the world. No plan is better than the others. Each one is good for a different life.

items.p: A starfish has 5 matching arms. A full turn is 360 degrees. How many degrees between neighbouring arms?
items.why: 360 divided by 5 is 72. Turn a starfish by 72 degrees and she looks the same as before.

items.p: The young form of an animal that looks very different from the adult is called a ____.
items.why: A caterpillar is the larva of a butterfly. A starfish larva is a tiny two-sided swimmer.

items.p: In Tall Cone or Coil, taller dough cones fell at smaller tilts. Explain why a taller cone falls sooner.
items.a: A taller cone has more of its weight high above the base. A small tilt carries that weight past the edge of the base, and then the cone tips over.
items.why: A strong answer talks about where the weight is and how wide the base is. 'It is taller' alone repeats the result without explaining it.

items.p: Unequal balls made the roller curve in the Lopsided Roller test. So why do fast animals have matching sides?
items.a: If the fins, legs or wings on one side pushed harder, the animal would curve as the roller did. Matching sides give equal pushes, so she can travel straight.
items.why: A strong answer carries the idea from the model to the animal: unequal pushes make a curve.

items.p: A jellyfish and a starfish are both built in rings. Give evidence that they are not close relatives.
items.a: A starfish larva has a front end and two matching sides, so starfish ancestors were two-sided. Genes also place starfish closer to fish than to jellyfish.
items.why: A strong answer names evidence other than the adult shape: the larva or the genes.

items.p: The cells of one muscle all lie in the same direction. Why does that help the muscle pull?
items.a: Each cell shortens along its length. When all the cells lie the same way, their small pulls add up in one direction.
items.why: A strong answer says that pulls in one direction add together. In Many Threads, One Lift, the threads held the bag only when they shared the pull.

items.p: Most starfish have five arms and not six. Scientists disagree about how to explain a feature like this.

views.says: Every feature is there because it helped the animal's ancestors. We should look for what five arms do better.
Some features are left over from an ancestor, or come from how a body grows. Five may have no special use.
We should test before we choose. Some starfish have more than five arms. Compare how well they move and feed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what evidence could change your mind.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that matching sides and coiled shells do have uses we can test. Another is that not every feature we test turns out to have a use.
items.why: Working scientists hold each of these views. A strong answer says what evidence would count against the view it chose.

items.p: Invent an animal who lives fixed to a rock in a stream. Draw the body plan and label the mouth.
items.a: For example, a cup-shaped animal with a ring of arms round a mouth on top. A second good answer is an animal with a wide net facing upstream. In a stream, food comes from one side.
items.why: A strong drawing fits the body to where the food comes from. A ring suits food from all sides. A stream brings food from one direction, so a body that faces upstream is also a good answer.

quiz.p: Which list names four animal body plans?
quiz.why: A body plan is a layout. Fur and feathers are coverings, running and swimming are ways to move, and egg to adult is a life cycle.

opts: Matching parts arranged round a middle
One left side and one right side
A body made of one cell
quiz.why: Radial symmetry is the ring plan. The parts are arranged round a middle point, like the spokes of a cycle wheel.

quiz.p: A jellyfish's mouth is under the middle of her body. Why does that suit a drifting life?
opts: Food can arrive from any side
quiz.why: A drifting animal meets the water equally on all sides. A mouth in the middle is the same distance from every tentacle.

quiz.p: What does every two-sided animal have?
opts: A front end and one middle line
quiz.why: A two-sided animal has a front end, a tail end and one line down the middle. The left and right sides on either side of that line match.

quiz.p: Why do matching left and right sides help an animal who travels?
opts: Both sides push equally, so she goes straight
quiz.why: If one side pushed harder, the animal would curve. Equal sides give equal pushes and a straight path.

quiz.p: A roller has a big left ball and a small right ball. Which way will it curve?
opts: To the right, towards the small ball
To the left, towards the big ball
quiz.why: The big ball covers more floor in each turn, so the left side gets ahead. The roller swings round towards the small ball.

opts: One of a row of repeated body parts
The front end of an animal
quiz.why: Segments are parts built on one pattern and repeated along the body, as in an earthworm or a centipede.

quiz.p: Which part of your own body is built in repeated segments?
quiz.why: Your backbone is a row of alike bones, and your ribs repeat in pairs. Humans are segmented animals on the inside.

quiz.p: Why does a snail's shell coil as the snail grows?
opts: A coil stays compact and easy to carry
The snail spins while she sleeps
quiz.why: The shell grows only at the opening, so it gets longer all the time. Coiling keeps that long cone low and compact.

quiz.p: Which of these is one of the four main kinds of animal tissue?
quiz.why: The four kinds are covering tissue, connecting tissue, muscle tissue and nerve tissue. A finger is a body part made of all four.

opts: A body part built from several tissues
quiz.why: An organ, such as a heart or an eye, is built from several tissues that work together.

quiz.p: A dolphin and a shark have the same body shape. Does this prove they are close relatives?
opts: No. Similar lives can give similar shapes
Yes. Both live in the sea
No. Sharks have no body plan
quiz.why: A dolphin is a mammal and a shark is a fish. Both swim fast, and fast swimming suits a smooth, pointed body. Shape alone does not prove family.

applications: Boats, cars, cycles and aeroplanes are built with matching left and right sides, so that they travel straight.
A train is built in segments. Coaches of one design are joined in a row, and a coach can be added or taken off.
Doctors look at a tiny piece of tissue under a microscope to find out whether the cells are healthy. This is called a biopsy.
Doctors can grow sheets of skin tissue from a few of a patient's own cells, to cover a bad burn.
Engineers build robots in segments, copied from worms and snakes, to crawl through pipes and fallen buildings.
A ceiling fan, an umbrella and a parisal are built in a ring. Each must work the same way on every side.

open_questions.q: Why do most starfish have five arms?
open_questions.why_open: Five-part bodies are very rare outside the starfish and sea urchin group. Nobody knows what first fixed the number at five, or whether five has any special use.

open_questions.q: Why do almost all snails coil to the right?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found a gene that sets the direction of the coil in pond snails. They do not know why the right-handed form became so common in nearly every kind of snail.

open_questions.q: What did the first two-sided animal look like?
open_questions.why_open: The animal lived more than 550 million years ago and was small and soft. Very few fossils of such animals exist, so scientists argue from genes and from a handful of traces in rock.

open_questions.q: Which animals are the oldest branch of the animal family tree, sponges or comb jellies?
open_questions.why_open: Comb jellies have nerves and muscles, and sponges have neither. A gene study in 2023 put comb jellies on the oldest branch, and other studies put sponges there. The answer changes how we think nerves began.

open_questions.q: Is most of a starfish's body really built like a head?
open_questions.why_open: A gene study in 2023 found head genes at work along every arm of a young starfish. Scientists are still checking this in other kinds of starfish and in sea urchins.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from the Lopsided Roller test, in centimetres from the line. The matched roller stopped at 6 left, 4 right, 9 right, 3 left and 5 left. The lopsided roller stopped at 38, 45, 41, 36 and 40, all to the right. Does the matched roller have a favourite side? Does the lopsided roller?
maths.answer: The matched roller has no favourite side. The lopsided roller always goes right.
maths.explain: The matched roller went left 3 times and right 2 times, and never more than 9 centimetres. That is what chance looks like. The lopsided roller went right all 5 times, by about 40 centimetres. Five out of five on one side, and far from the line, points to a cause in the roller.
maths.context: In the Lopsided Roller test you roll a pencil with a ball of dough on each end. You measure how far from a straight line it stops.
maths.why_maths: Looking at the sides as well as the sizes of the numbers separates a chance wobble from a real turn.

maths.problem: In a made-up run of Tall Cone or Coil, the 6 centimetre cone fell at a lift of 18 centimetres. The 9 centimetre cone fell at 14 centimetres, and the 12 centimetre cone at 10 centimetres. What is the pattern? Predict the lift for a 15 centimetre cone.
maths.answer: Each extra 3 centimetres of cone makes it fall 4 centimetres sooner. A 15 centimetre cone should fall at about 6 centimetres.
maths.explain: 18 minus 14 is 4, and 14 minus 10 is 4. So the next step is 10 minus 4, which is 6. This is a prediction from a pattern. Real cones may not follow it exactly, so the next thing to do is to test it.
maths.context: In Tall Cone or Coil you stand dough cones on a board and lift one end until each cone falls.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the results lets you predict a shape you have not tested, and a prediction can be checked.

maths.problem: A house centipede has 15 segments with legs, and one pair of legs on each. How many legs does she have? Every centipede has an odd number of pairs of legs. Can any centipede have exactly 100 legs?
maths.answer: The house centipede has 30 legs. No centipede has exactly 100 legs.
maths.explain: 15 pairs is 15 times 2, which is 30 legs. For 100 legs a centipede would need 100 divided by 2, which is 50 pairs. But 50 is an even number, and centipedes always have an odd number of pairs.
maths.context: In One Segment, Many Times you cut a paper animal with one pair of legs on every segment. A centipede is built this way.
maths.why_maths: Because the legs come in pairs on segments, dividing by two tells you how many segments carry legs.

maths.problem: A moon jellyfish has 4 matching parts round her middle. One kind of coral polyp has 8 tentacles round the mouth. A full turn is 360 degrees. How far must each animal be turned to look the same as before?
maths.answer: The jellyfish 90 degrees, and the coral polyp 45 degrees.
maths.explain: 360 divided by 4 is 90. 360 divided by 8 is 45. The more matching parts a ring animal has, the smaller the turn that brings her back to the same look.
maths.context: In Three Pairs of Sides you turned an upside-down tumbler and found it the same all the way round. Ring animals have a fixed number of matching parts.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a full turn by the number of parts gives a number that describes a ring body exactly.

maths.problem: In a made-up game of Sit or Seek, the ring animal ate 8 pieces of drifting food in 12 turns. The front animal ate 2 in 12 turns. What fraction of the turns did each animal eat on? How many times as much did the ring animal eat?
maths.answer: The ring animal ate on two thirds of the turns and the front animal on one sixth. The ring animal ate 4 times as much.
maths.explain: 8 out of 12 is the same as 2 out of 3. 2 out of 12 is the same as 1 out of 6. 8 divided by 2 is 4. The ring animal has four sides ready and the front animal has one. So four times as much is what the rules lead us to expect.
maths.context: In Sit or Seek a die decides which side food drifts in from. A ring animal catches food on every side, and a front animal only on the side she faces.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you compare the two bodies fairly. You can also check the scores against what the rules should give.

maths.problem: In a made-up run of Many Threads, One Lift, one thread snapped at about 500 grams. The bag weighs 2 kilograms. What is the smallest number of threads that could hold it? Why might a builder still need 6?
maths.answer: 4 threads at the least. More may be needed because threads rarely share the weight equally.
maths.explain: 2 kilograms is 2000 grams. 2000 divided by 500 is 4. That works only if every thread carries an equal share. If one thread is a little shorter, it carries more than 500 grams and snaps first. Extra threads give a margin.
maths.context: In Many Threads, One Lift you lift a 2 kilogram bag with sewing thread. The threads are a model of the fibres in a tendon.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the load by the strength of one thread gives the least number of fibres needed. It also shows why real tissues have many spare.
