how_we_found_out.story: In 1817 the French scientist Georges Cuvier sorted all animals into four groups by the layout of their bodies. He put starfish and jellyfish together in one group, called Radiata, because both are built in rings. For about thirty years most scientists agreed that ring-shaped animals were one family. In the 1840s the German scientist Johannes Müller towed a fine net through the sea near the island of Heligoland. He looked at his catch under a microscope. He found tiny, clear swimmers, each with a front end and two matching sides. He kept watching them. Inside each swimmer a small five-part star grew, and the two-sided body shrank away. The swimmers were young starfish and young sea urchins. So a starfish begins life with two sides, as a worm or a fish does. In 1848 Rudolf Leuckart split Cuvier's ring group into separate groups. Today scientists also compare genes. The genes show that starfish are closer relatives of fish and humans than of jellyfish.
how_we_found_out.who: Georges Cuvier in France, then Johannes Müller and Rudolf Leuckart in Germany
how_we_found_out.when: Cuvier published his four groups in 1817. Müller studied the larvae in the 1840s, and Leuckart split the ring group in 1848.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That all ring-shaped animals are one family. Müller found that a starfish begins life as a two-sided larva. So the ring shape of a starfish and the ring shape of a jellyfish arose separately.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist of the 1840s at a table by a window over the sea, looking through a brass microscope, with a glass dish of sea water and a fine net beside him.

roots.context: In this unit you rolled a lopsided roller, tilted dough shells and found four tissues in your hand. Here we ask what the shape of a body tells us about the life that body leads.

deep_truth.truth: In the Lopsided Roller test, the roller with unequal balls curved the same way on every roll. An animal who travels needs equal pushes on her left and right, so those two sides match. Her top and bottom differ, and her front and back differ, because gravity and travel treat them differently. So the layout of a body shows which directions matter in that animal's life.
deep_truth.habit: We treat an animal's shape as a fact about the animal alone, like a name. The shape also describes the animal's world: where food comes from, which way gravity pulls, and which way she travels.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Lopsided Roller test, only the roller with matching balls went nearly straight. A sea anemone, who meets food from every side, is the same all the way round. A starfish larva who swims one way has two sides. The adult, who can creep any way, has five arms.

three.who_am_i: Your face is at your front because your ancestors travelled head first. Your backbone repeats like the segments of a worm. Your hand holds the same four tissues as a frog's foot.
three.what_is_life: Life builds millions of different bodies from a few layouts and four kinds of tissue. Each layout fits one way of meeting the world.
three.what_is_this_world: Gravity, water and the direction of travel leave their mark on every body. You can read part of an animal's world from the animal's shape.

roots.thread: The first animals were small groups of cells. Their descendants became rings, two-sided swimmers, coiled snails and long rows of segments. Under these different layouts, the same family of genes still marks head from tail in flies, mice and children. Many wise teachers taught that one life takes many forms. The science here makes a similar point in a precise way. Every animal body plan grew from one beginning, and the shared genes still show it.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son that by knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot and the plate differ in name and shape, and the clay is the same.
teachings.link: The verse is about the ground of all things, and it does not mention animals. A prawn's body shows the same idea in a small way. Her feelers, jaws and legs are one repeated part, shaped differently on each segment.

teachings.source: D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1917), chapter 1
teachings.teaching: Thompson wrote that the form of any object, living or not, is a 'diagram of forces'. He meant that a shape shows the pushes and pulls that made it.
teachings.link: The Lopsided Roller test and Tall Cone or Coil both show a shape answering a force. Matching sides answer the need for equal pushes. A low coil answers the pull of gravity on a tall shell.

science.text: The same family of Hox genes marks out head to tail in flies, mice and humans. This is strong evidence that these very different bodies come from one ancestor.
A study of starfish genes in 2023 suggested that most of a starfish's body is built like a head, with almost no trunk. Scientists are still testing this.

other_view.who: Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin, in a paper of 1979
other_view.view: They warned against explaining every feature of a body by its usefulness. Some features are left over from ancestors, and some are side effects of how a body grows. On this view a starfish's five arms may have no special reason. We should not read a purpose into every shape.

practice.title: Find your middle line
practice.say: Stand still and close your eyes. Put one finger on the top of your head. Draw it slowly down your forehead, your nose, your chin and your chest to your navel. That is your middle line. Now lift both arms and feel that they weigh the same. Take one slow breath in and out. Then turn once round on the spot, slowly. Notice that you must turn to face each wall. A sea anemone never needs to turn.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Draw a finger from your head down to your navel. Lift both arms. Feel that they match. Turn slowly round once. What did you do to face each wall?

ask: Your face is at your front because your ancestors travelled head first. Where might your eyes be if humans had always lived fixed in one spot?
In the Lopsided Roller test, the shape of the roller decided the path. How much of what you do is decided by the shape of your body?
A starfish has two sides when young and five arms when grown. Which shape is the starfish?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use each part, step by step. It has not yet been done at home. The Lopsided Roller test (core) needs stiff atta dough or modelling clay, three pencils, a tray and a thin book. It also needs about one and a half metres of smooth floor. Soft dough flattens and will not roll, so knead in dry atta until a ball keeps its shape. The matched roller should stop within about 10 centimetres of the line. The 4 and 3 roller should curve widely towards the small ball. The 4 and 2 roller should turn in a tight circle. If the rollers stop too soon, raise the ramp on a second book. Wipe the flour off the floor afterwards. Tall Cone or Coil (core) uses the same dough, a board about 30 centimetres long and a ruler. The heights in the example table are made up. Real cones are never perfect, so your numbers will differ. The taller cone should still fall first, and the coil should not fall. If a cone slides before it falls, put a sheet of paper under it. Four Tissues in Your Hand needs only a hand, a feather or thread and a drop of water. One Segment, Many Times needs scissors. Eight layers of paper are stiff to cut, so a grown-up may need to help. Plan Families needs two players for the asking game, and has a sorting version for one child. Sit or Seek was checked by working out the chances. In the drifting sea the ring animal eats about 8 of 12 and the front animal about 2. In the still sea the front animal eats 3 or 4 and the ring animal 0 or 1. Many Threads, One Lift needs a grown-up for the first lift. Thread strength varies a lot, so add or remove weight until one thread just snaps. Prawn, Fish and Shell is only for families who have a prawn, a piece of fish or a shell. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Some facts need care. 'About ninety-nine of every hundred kinds of animals are two-sided' is the usual rounded figure. Müller's work on larvae began in the 1840s and ran on into the 1850s. The usual explanation is that coiling keeps a shell compact and easy to carry. The unit gives this as what scientists think. The claim that a starfish is mostly a head comes from one study of 2023 and is marked as debated. The unit names the rare valampuri sangu without saying whether it is left-handed or right-handed. The temple way of naming and the scientists' way of naming differ. The Chandogya verse is given as a paraphrase, and the unit says plainly that the verse is not about animals.
